title: Tone and Shifts in Tone
short: Tone is the writer’s attitude, shown by diction and sentence structure. Analysis often turns on where the tone shifts.
trouble: Learners name a tone with a vague word (positive, negative) instead of a precise one (wry, urgent, reverent).

blocks.html: Tone is the writer’s attitude toward the subject and the audience: the voice you would hear if the text were read aloud. It is built from patterns, word choice (diction) and sentence structure.
Name tone with a precise word (reverent, urgent, indignant, wry), point to the words that create it, and watch for where it shifts. A shift usually marks a turn in the writer’s purpose.

Tone tells readers how to take the words. “Nice job” can be praise or sarcasm; only tone decides. In analysis, a tone shift is often the most important moment in a text, because the writer has changed what they want from the audience.

head: Instead of
Try
rows: admiring, hopeful, celebratory, grateful, reverent, warm
indignant, bitter, scornful, mournful, anxious, disappointed

blocks.title: A shift in Douglass
blocks.q: Douglass opens: “I do not remember ever to have appeared as a speaker before any assembly more shrinkingly, nor with greater distrust of my ability, than I do this day.” Later: “At a time like this, scorching irony, not convincing argument, is needed.” Name the tones and the shift.
steps: The opening is humble and self-doubting: words like “shrinkingly” and “distrust of my ability.”
The later line is fierce and defiant: “scorching irony” and the bold declaration of what is needed.
The shift from humble to indignant marks his turn from greeting a friendly audience to indicting the nation’s hypocrisy.
blocks.a: From humble and modest to indignant and defiant; the shift marks the speech’s turn to its real purpose.

blocks.title: Tone from word choice
blocks.q: Lincoln, 1865: “Fondly do we hope—fervently do we pray—that this mighty scourge of war may speedily pass away.” What is the tone?
steps: “Hope” and “pray,” with “fondly” and “fervently,” are words of longing and faith.
“Scourge” treats the war as a punishment to be endured, not a victory to celebrate.
The tone is solemn and prayerful, not triumphant, even though the war was nearly won.
blocks.a: Solemn and prayerful; Lincoln avoids triumph on purpose.

blocks.html: Naming a tone with a vague word, such as positive, negative or emotional. Every text is one of these, so the word tells your reader nothing. Check: could your tone word describe a birthday card and a eulogy equally well? If so, find a sharper one, and quote the words that prove it.

opts.source: Frederick Douglass, Fourth of July oration, Rochester, 1852 (opening, then a later passage)

sentences.text: He who could address this audience without a quailing sensation, has stronger nerves than I have.
The task before me is one which requires much previous thought and study for its proper performance.
At a time like this, scorching irony, not convincing argument, is needed.
We need the storm, the whirlwind, and the earthquake.

blocks.cap: The tone shifts from humble to indignant.
